Two of the most famous synthesizers ever made are close relatives. The **Minimoog Model D** (Moog, 1970) put a modular synth's
oscillators, filter and envelopes behind fixed switches in a box you could take on stage. The **Prophet-5** (Sequential
Circuits, 1978) did almost the same thing five times over, one voice per note, and added a microprocessor that remembered
every knob. On this page each is rebuilt in the browser. You can turn a sound on one into the nearest sound on the other and
read what happened to every setting: **the same**, **close** or **impossible**, and why.

Both panels here are drawn after the real ones and are not copies; the names belong to their makers. Every fact about the
real instruments comes from their manuals and is cited with its page. Anything the manuals do not say, such as how a
Prophet knob numbered 0 to 10 maps to hertz, is this page's own choice and is marked so.

## The two synths

<div class="scmp"></div>

**How to use it.** Pick an **Example**, then press **▶ Model D**, **▶ Prophet-5** or **▶ One, then the other**. Turn any
knob on the top panel and the bottom one follows. **Turn into the …** makes the other synth the starting point. Point at a
line of the report to light up the controls it is about on both panels. Coloured outlines on the panels show
<span class="scmp-tag scmp-exact">the same</span>, <span class="scmp-tag scmp-approx">close</span> and
<span class="scmp-tag scmp-lost">cannot be done</span>.

## The Model D patch sheets

The Model D manual ends with patch sheets: a drawing of the front panel for each sound, with orange pointers on the knobs,
light-blue circles round the chosen range and wave, and the switches coloured on the side that is pressed (Moog Music,
*Minimoog Model D* manual, pp. 55–76; blank sheets to copy on pp. 77–79). Below, each one is redrawn in the same layout.
Pick a sheet, turn the knobs on it, press **▶ Play** to hear it on the Model D panel above, or **Show on the panel above** to
compare it knob by knob. **One part at a time** shows a single section with **Back** and **Next**; **Large print** and
**High contrast** make it easier to read. The readings were taken from the printed pages to the nearest half mark; the ones
that were hard to read are listed under the sheet. Times on the contour knobs follow the printed scale (10 ms to 10 s); how
the cutoff knob maps to hertz is this page's choice, as on the panel above.

<div class="moog-sheets"></div>

## What they share

Both are **subtractive synths** ([Sound 7](sound-subtractive.qmd)). Oscillators make a wave full of harmonics, a mixer
blends them, and a **4-pole, 24 dB-per-octave low-pass filter** takes harmonics away. One envelope moves the filter and
another moves the loudness. On both, resonance can be turned up until the filter whistles by itself. So a plain bass or
lead translates almost knob for knob: try **Fat bass** and look at how few red lines there are. The filter plot shows two
curves with the same slope. The difference is in how they *sound* when pushed, because the filters are different
circuits: the Moog **ladder**, and on the Prophet-5 either Dave Rossum's SSI 2140 (the sound of the first Prophets, "Rev
1/2") or Doug Curtis's CEM 3320 ("Rev 3"). Flip the Prophet's **Rev** switch and listen.

## What only the Model D can do

- **Three oscillators on every note.** A Prophet voice has two. The **Lead in fifths and fourths** example (from the Model D
  manual) tunes oscillator 2 a fifth up and oscillator 3 a fourth down, so each key plays a three-note chord. On the
  Prophet-5 the third pitch is gone. Its **Chord memory** can hold such a stack, but only by playing it with several voices.
- **Feeding its own output back in.** With nothing plugged into its external input, the Model D's output runs back into
  its mixer. Turn that input up and the mixer **overloads**, which makes a growling, compressed sound. Watch the
  **Mixer drive** plot bend over in **Overdriven bass**. The Prophet's mixer can also be driven hard, but it has no path
  from its output back to its input.
- **A spare oscillator as the modulator.** Oscillator 3 can leave the keyboard and run as a slow LFO, or at audio speed
  for FM, while oscillators 1 and 2 sound. On the Prophet the only oscillator that can modulate is B, so once B is busy
  sounding there is nothing left.

## What only the Prophet-5 can do

- **Chords.** Five voices, so five notes at once. Play **String pad** on both and the Model D keeps only the lowest
  note, which is how a classic Model D chooses.
- **Hard sync.** Oscillator A restarts every time oscillator B does. Sweeping A's pitch with the filter envelope through
  Poly Mod gives the famous tearing lead (**Hard-sync lead**, from the Prophet's guide). The Model D has no sync.
- **Moving pulse width.** The Prophet's pulse width is a knob that the LFO or Poly Mod can sweep, which gives the
  chorused, shimmering tone of **Pulse-width-modulated strings**. The Model D's pulse widths are fixed positions of a
  switch.
- **Poly Mod.** Every voice's filter envelope or oscillator B can modulate its own oscillator A or filter. That is
  sync sweeps and FM *in chords*. The Model D can do FM (**Oscillator 3 frequency-modulating oscillator 1**), but for one
  note, with the depth on the mod wheel.
- **Memory.** The Prophet stores its sounds as programs (the original held 40). A Model D sound exists only while the
  knobs stay where they are.

## What only the TB-303 can do

- **Accent and slide on each step.** The TB-303's sequencer stores pitch, length, accent and slide for every step (TB-303
  manual p. 89). An accented step is louder and brighter by as much as the ACCENT knob says (p. 34). A slide step glides into
  the next one. Try **Acid line** and translate it: no other synth here has accent, so it becomes velocity at best.
- **Almost nothing else.** One oscillator with two waveforms and five tone knobs (p. 34). The lesson goes the other way:
  most patches from the other synths lose a great deal on the 303. Its filter is a 24 dB low-pass that does not whistle on
  its own (Wikipedia; unverified).

## What only the Juno-60 can do

- **The chorus.** Chorus I, or the stronger II, is built in (Juno-60 manual p. 22). Every other synth here loses it in
  **PWM strings with chorus II**.
- **A sub-oscillator and a high-pass filter** next to one DCO (pp. 13-14). The Juno-106's HPF at 0 boosts the bass instead
  (Juno-106 manual p. 18), and the 106 adds portamento, which the Juno-60's DCO does not have (Juno-60 p. 12; Juno-106 p. 23):
  flip **Model** to 106.
- **One envelope for everything.** Filter and loudness share one ADSR (p. 16), so patches from synths with two envelopes
  lose one of them.

## What only the ARP 2600 can do

- **Patch cords on top of the normals.** Every input of the 2600 already has a connection inside, which a cord replaces
  (2600 M manual pp. 5-15). VCO-2's sine reaches VCO-1, VCO-3 and the filter; sample-and-hold reaches every VCO. **Patch
  cords** on the panel add routes the other synths have no names for.
- **A ring modulator, sample-and-hold and three VCOs that can each be an LFO** (pp. 6-9, 15). Try **Ring-modulator bells**
  and **Sample-and-hold bleeps**.
- **Two envelopes of different kinds:** an ADSR and an AR, the VCA taking one linearly and the other exponentially (p. 12).

## What only the OB-Xa can do

- **A 2-pole filter as well as a 4-pole one.** The 4-POLE switch chooses 24 dB per octave (fuller), or 12 dB (brighter)
  when it is off (OB-Xa manual p. 11). Translate **2-pole brass pad** and compare the slopes on the filter plot.
- **Filter envelope on oscillator 2,** up to an octave, with sync (p. 10): **Sync lead**.
- **The SEM's filter modes.** The SEM's filter could be low-pass, band-pass, high-pass or notch (Wikipedia; unverified).
  The extra **SEM mode** switch is not on the OB-Xa. A band-pass patch is lost on every low-pass-only synth.

## What only the MS-20 can do

- **A resonant high-pass and low-pass filter in series**, each able to oscillate (MS-20 manual p. 5): **Screaming HP + LP**.
  Only the Juno also has a high-pass filter, and its filter has no resonance.
- **A patch panel, EG 1 with a delay, and EG 2 with a hold time** (pp. 6-7). Nothing else here delays a pitch sweep or holds a
  note after the key lifts.

## What only the DX7 can do

- **FM.** Six sine-wave operators, each with its own envelope of four rates and four levels, wired into one of 32 algorithms
  (DX7 manual pp. 23-26). The manual's first exercise sounds like "a saw-tooth wave which is going through a filter that has a
  lot of resonance" with "no filters involved" (p. 35). That one translates. **Bell** and **Electric-piano-like tine** do not:
  on every other synth the FM note in the report is red, and only an oscillator per carrier is left. This is the point of the
  comparison.
- **Sixteen voices** (PDF p. 4). Going the other way, the DX7 loses every filter, resonance and pulse-width setting, because
  there is nothing to set.

## What only the PPG Wave can do

- **Wavetables.** Each oscillator steps through a table of 64 waves, and an envelope or the LFO can move it (Sound On Sound's
  Wave 2.3 review): **Wavetable sweep by envelope**. Other synths keep one fixed wave. The page's four tables are its own,
  not the PPG's.
- Into **analog 24 dB filters** (SSM 2044, PPG Wave 2.3 service manual p. 5; Wikipedia). No owner's manual was found, so the
  panel layout is this page's (unverified).

## Why they differ

The Model D manual calls it "a direct descendant of the Moog modular synthesizers". In place of patch cables it uses
colour-coded rocker switches: orange to connect modulation, blue to turn sounds on and off, white for performance features
and black to choose between sources (Model D manual p. 15). That made it fast to set up on stage, and it played one note.
Dave Smith, who designed the Prophet-5, writes that he "had the notion that these new-ish things called microprocessors
might be useful in designing … a fully programmable polyphonic synthesizer — the first of its kind" (Prophet-5 guide p. x).
The 1981 technical manual describes a Z-80 microprocessor scanning the keys, sharing them out among five voices and keeping 40
programs in memory.

This page's own reading, not from either manual, is that a microprocessor and five copies of a voice explain most of the
lists above. Two oscillators a voice rather than three kept five voices affordable, and Poly Mod put a modulating
oscillator, like the Model D's third, back inside every voice.

## History, players and records

Facts in this section are from Wikipedia's articles on each synth and the sources they cite (listed below).

### Minimoog Model D

- **Made:** introduced in 1970, designed by Bill Hemsath and other engineers with Robert Moog; prototypes A to C came first
  and the Model D in early 1970. Produced from 1970 to 1981, over 12,000 in 13 years. Reissued in 2016–17 and again in 2022.
- **Firsts:** the first synthesizer sold in ordinary retail shops, and the first with a pitch wheel.
- **Styles:** first popular in progressive rock and jazz, then disco, pop, rock, electronic music and funk.
- **Players and records:** Sun Ra's *My Brother the Wind* (1970), perhaps its first recording. Rick Wakeman used five on stage;
  Keith Emerson played one. Herbie Hancock, Chick Corea and Dick Hyman were early jazz users, and Stevie Wonder used it. The bass of
  Parliament's "Flash Light". Kraftwerk's *Autobahn* (1974) and *The Man-Machine* (1978). In disco, ABBA and Giorgio Moroder. In
  electronic music, Tangerine Dream, Klaus Schulze and Gary Numan.

### Prophet-5

- **Made:** designed by Dave Smith and John Bowen in 1977 and shown at the NAMM show in January 1978: the first polyphonic synth
  with fully programmable memory. Rev 1 (182 made), Rev 2, and Rev 3 (almost 6,000, on CEM chips), made from 1978 to 1984; Rev 4
  in 2020. It cost US$3,995 (Rev 1 and 2) and $4,595 (Rev 3).
- **Players and records:** Greg Hawkes of the Cars on "Let's Go" (1979) and "Shake It Up" (1981). Phil Collins, "In the Air
  Tonight" (1981). Japan, "Ghosts" (1982). Michael Jackson's *Thriller* (1982), Madonna's *Like a Virgin* (1984), Peter Gabriel's
  *So* (1986), Radiohead's *Kid A*, including "Everything In Its Right Place". Kraftwerk took it on their 1981 *Computer World* tour;
  Ryuichi Sakamoto used it on *Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence* and with Yellow Magic Orchestra.
- **Film:** Vangelis, *Blade Runner* (1982); Brad Fiedel, *The Terminator* (1984, on a Prophet-10); John Carpenter.

## Build it from a video

Each video below rebuilds a famous record's sound on the real instrument. Watch it, press **Build …** for the song (that fills in
the form), set the panel the way the video does, listen, and press **Download the patch file**. Write in the notes what you had to
guess: a video shows the knobs, but this page's knobs are not the real ones (see [What is checked](#what-is-checked-and-what-is-not)).
Your teacher adds the files to the **Library** under the synths, marked *settings from the video (student)* until checked against
the record. Use **Open a patch file** to load one again.

## Reading the pictures

- **Signal flow** (inside each panel): oscillators and noise into the mixer, then the filter and the amplifier, with the
  modulation wires drawn and lit while they act. A wire or box drawn in **red** is a part of the starting patch that the
  other synth cannot copy.
- **Filter**: how loud each frequency comes out of each synth's filter with its current knobs, for middle C. The resonance
  peak and the 24 dB slope are drawn from the engine's own filter model, simplified to a straight-line (linear) version,
  so overload is not shown.
- **Envelopes**: both synths' filter envelopes (thin lines) and loudness envelopes (thick lines) for a key held one
  second. Flip the Prophet's **Rev** switch to see its envelope change from curved to almost straight, as the Prophet's
  guide describes.
- **Mixer drive**: what the mixer does to a signal as it gets louder. The line stays straight while the sound is clean,
  then flattens at the top once the mixer overloads.
- **Scope and spectrum**: the waves as they sound, and their harmonics.

## What is checked and what is not

Checked against the manuals: every control's name, the waves and ranges each oscillator has, the filter types and their
slope, envelope stages, LFO rates and shapes, which sources can modulate which targets, voices and unison, the pitch wheel
ranges, glide, the Model D's feedback path and its default low-note priority. Each line of the report names its page.

This page's own choices, not from the manuals: how the Prophet's 0 to 10 knobs map to hertz, seconds and octaves; the
curves between the Model D's printed end points; the exact widths of the Model D's "wide" and "narrow" pulses; the shape of
its triangle-sawtooth wave; modulation depths; unison detune in cents; and how the three filters differ (one model with
three settings, not simulations of the real circuits). Nobody has yet compared these sounds with the real instruments.
